title: GIFT City Just Got Its First US Company Listing. Here Is What NRIs Need to Know.
excerpt: Banking assets at $111 billion, US stocks now accessible, and the first American IPO on Indian exchanges — India's answer to Dubai and Singapore is crossing a threshold.
body:
India's GIFT City, the gleaming financial district rising between Ahmedabad and Gandhinagar, has spent years trying to convince global investors it is more than a policy experiment. This week, several developments suggest it may finally be crossing that threshold.

A US-headquartered company filed to list on GIFT City's exchanges for the first time. A major Indian trading platform launched direct access to US stocks through the GIFT City framework. And banking assets in the zone have crossed $111 billion. For NRIs who have watched from abroad as India built this rival to Dubai and Singapore, the question is shifting from "will it work?" to "is it too early or too late to act?"

## Tryfacta: The First US Company to List in India

Tryfacta, a workforce solutions provider headquartered in Dublin, California, has filed draft papers for an IPO on GIFT City's NSE IFSC and India International Exchange. If approved, it would become the first US-headquartered company to list on an Indian exchange. The company, founded in 1996 by Ratika and Adesh Tyagi, provides AI-driven staffing solutions to US federal agencies across 41 states. Its net revenue climbed to $50.5 million in fiscal 2025 from $35 million two years earlier.

The significance is not in Tryfacta's size but in the precedent. A US company choosing to raise capital through India's financial infrastructure — in dollars, on Indian exchanges — validates the plumbing that GIFT City has spent years building. The issue will be denominated in US dollars. Indian retail investors can participate through the Reserve Bank's Liberalised Remittance Scheme, which caps outward remittances at $250,000 per person per financial year.

## US Stock Access Through GIFT City

Separately, Dhan, one of India's prominent trading platforms, launched investment access to US-listed stocks and ETFs through its GIFT City subsidiary, Raise IFSC Private Limited. Indian investors can now buy Nasdaq and NYSE-listed securities through the Dhan app, with brokerage fixed at 0.25 per cent and no custody fees. The platform will also offer systematic investment plans in US stocks, a feature designed for the drip-feed investment style that Indian retail investors have embraced in domestic mutual funds.

For NRIs, this is significant not because they need a new way to buy US stocks — most already have US brokerage accounts — but because it signals that GIFT City is developing the kind of two-way capital flow infrastructure that makes a financial hub genuinely useful. Money can now flow from India to the US and, through listings like Tryfacta, from the US to India, all within one regulatory framework.

## The Tax Advantage That Just Got Bigger

India last week exempted foreign institutional investors from capital gains tax on government securities, a move explicitly designed to attract stable foreign capital as the rupee has weakened over five per cent this year. While India's Chief Economic Adviser V. Anantha Nageswaran said on Friday that the case for similar equity tax changes is weaker, the bond tax exemption directly benefits GIFT City's positioning as an offshore investment gateway.

Entities operating within GIFT City already enjoy exemptions from securities transaction tax, certain capital gains benefits, and tax holidays. In April, the International Financial Services Centres Authority approved the first Foreign Family Investment Fund under its 2025 regulations — a milestone that validates GIFT City for family offices, cross-border estate planning, and global wealth structures.

## The Honest Assessment

For all the momentum, a realistic assessment requires acknowledging what GIFT City is not. It is not yet Dubai or Singapore. Liquidity across its exchanges is improving but still trails established global markets. The ecosystem of banks, asset managers, and insurers is expanding but remains thinner than mature hubs. Singapore's High Commissioner to India highlighted "increasing Singaporean investment" in GIFT City in May, but that diplomatic endorsement reflects potential more than present depth.

"We are not trying to make another Singapore or Hong Kong or Dubai," IFSCA Chairman Kaul said this week. "We are creating an organic ecosystem of global standards where global talent are comfortable." The planned additions — a sports arena, hospitality properties, a golf range, metro connectivity — suggest the zone is thinking in decades, not quarters.

For NRI investors, the practical framework is this: GIFT City is not a replacement for existing global allocations. It is a complementary layer — a tax-efficient, India-linked base for portfolio diversification, offshore fund structuring, and succession planning. The asymmetry lies in timing. Entering while the ecosystem is still developing means navigating early-stage friction but gaining positioning before the infrastructure matures and the advantages narrow.

Geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East has also prompted some NRI investors to reconsider regional concentration risk. GIFT City is increasingly viewed not as a competitor to Dubai but as a diversification option alongside it — an India-aligned hub that does not require choosing one jurisdiction over another.

The bottom line: GIFT City is no longer a concept. It is a functioning financial district with $111 billion in banking assets, its first incoming US listing, and tax advantages that just expanded. Whether it reaches the scale of established hubs remains an open question. But the window for early positioning is demonstrably open — and the building is happening whether diaspora investors participate or not.

*Sources: Bar & Bench, The Hindu Business Line, Reuters, Outlook Business*
